clue.text: Fawley's touring capital, coming back and not forgetting

definitions.note: a phrase describing the faculty rather than a noun

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go all round it, so one piece wraps around the other
something coming back travels the opposite way, so the word is read from right to left

blocks.note: Fawley is the setter, so the setter's thing is 'my' thing
the Italian capital city

explanation.surface: The setter goes on a tour of a capital city and comes home with every detail still in mind.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter's name in the clue stands for the setter, and the possessive gives MY; MY goes round ROME read backwards to make MEMORY.
explanation.definitionFit: The ability to retain what happened is the faculty that keeps a person from losing things from mind.

clue.text: Way cut could be announced?

indicators.note: an announcement is spoken, so the sound of the word matters rather than its spelling

blocks.note: grass that has been cut has been mowed

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether the route for a cut could be read out.
explanation.definitionFit: A mode is a manner or method of doing something, a common synonym for a way.

clue.text: Demonstration about possible head of state

indicators.note: the demonstration word sits about, that is surrounding, the short word for regarding

blocks.note: a protest march is a demonstration
'on' means about, as in a talk on a subject

explanation.surface: A protest is held concerning someone who might become a country's leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' does double duty: it is a two-letter word meaning concerning, and its position says where that word goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A king or queen heads a state, but heads of state can also be presidents, hence the qualifier 'possible'.

clue.text: Jack suggested making statement very quickly

definitions.text: Jack suggested making statement very quickly

blocks.note: surface: a man called Jack proposed something
setter's reading: the surname completing the phrase people use for doing something in an instant

explanation.surface: A man named Jack recommends saying something in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'before you can say Jack Robinson' means extremely quickly; the answer is the second half of the name you would say.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase about saying a man's full name stands for instant speed, so his surname completes the saying.

clue.text: Large stone lion, possibly circled by winged creature

indicators.note: 'possibly' says the letters might be arranged some other way
to be circled by something is to have it wrapped all round you

blocks.note: a moth is a winged insect
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A big stone statue of a lion has an insect fluttering around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A monolith is a single great block of rock, often standing upright as a monument.

clue.text: It's nasty being stifled by pong up on a farm - apology offered?

indicators.note: what is stifled is smothered, held inside whatever stifles it
in a down entry, going up means the letters run from bottom to top
in a down entry, one part placed on another comes above it

blocks.note: BO, body odour, is a pong or bad smell
evil means wicked or nasty
a ranch is a large farm

explanation.surface: Something unpleasant is smothered by farmyard stink, and someone tries to say sorry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses the stifled chunk as a whole, not just the smell; 'It's' simply joins the clue together.
explanation.definitionFit: Holding out an olive branch is the traditional gesture of making peace, so it is a conciliatory overture or apology.

clue.text: The last bit of beef soup

blocks.note: an ox is a beef animal
the tail is the rearmost part of an animal

explanation.surface: Someone is told the very end of the beef goes into the soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The last bit of beef' reads naturally as leftovers, but it is the rear end of the animal: the ox's tail.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxtail is a thick, rich British broth made by stewing the tail of cattle.

clue.text: One wise person has kept popular original Lennon LP

indicators.note: something that has kept another item holds it inside

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
a mage is a learned magician or sage
what is in is fashionable or popular

explanation.surface: A sage has held on to a first pressing of a popular John Lennon record.
explanation.definitionFit: Imagine was John Lennon's celebrated 1971 solo album, named after its title song.

clue.text: Acts in support of maybe favourite type of fun

indicators.note: in a down entry, a supporting part sits underneath the part it holds up

blocks.note: the favourite in a race is perhaps a horse
a play is made up of acts

explanation.surface: Performers back the crowd's favourite kind of entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'favourite' looks like an adjective meaning best-loved, but it is the horse tipped to win a race.
explanation.definitionFit: Horseplay is rough, boisterous fun, the rowdy pushing and shoving of high spirits.

clue.text: Current unemployment benefit received by European?

indicators.note: whatever is received is taken in, so it sits inside the receiver

blocks.note: a Dane is a person from Denmark
UB is the abbreviation for unemployment benefit

explanation.surface: A European is asked whether they are currently getting the dole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like 'present-day', but it means a flowing body of water: the river Danube.
explanation.definitionFit: A river is a flowing current of water, and the Danube is Europe's second-longest river.

clue.text: Tune for broadcasting as some planes are refuelled

blocks.note: an air is a melody
to air a programme is to broadcast it

explanation.surface: A song is chosen for the radio while aircraft take on fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: In-flight refuelling passes fuel from one aircraft to another while both are flying, an operation between craft in the sky.

clue.text: Hair restorer?

blocks.note: surface: a tonic that makes hair grow back on a bald head
setter's reading: an unorthodox remedy, punning on the hair cut over the forehead

explanation.walkthrough: Alternative remedies are called fringe medicine; a fringe is also the hair over the forehead, so a cure for hair could be one.
explanation.definitionFit: Unconventional treatments outside mainstream practice are known as fringe medicine, and a fringe is a front section of hair.

clue.text: Agree to differ over a pint, hosting a very, very zealous individual

indicators.note: making the letters differ means changing their order
a host has guests inside, so the drink holds the following letters
in a down entry, one part placed over another comes first

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a pint is a glass of beer in a British pub
A as written plus V, the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: Two people agree to disagree over a drink with a fanatical acquaintance.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'very' splits: the first goes with 'a' into the wordplay, the second belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An eager beaver is an idiom for an enthusiastic, hard-working person, someone keen to the point of excess.

clue.text: Sometimes she misses getting registered

blocks.note: surface: a woman who occasionally fails to sign up
setter's reading: a young female pupil whose name is called at the morning register

explanation.surface: An absent-minded woman occasionally fails to get her name on the list.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Misses' reads as a verb, failing, but it is also the plural of 'Miss', how a girl at school is addressed; schools take a register of pupils each day.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl at school is one of the misses whose attendance is recorded on the class register.

clue.text: Keep wine for sale in Cheshire location

blocks.note: a shop that keeps an item has it in stock
port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: A shop in Cheshire stocks wine to sell.
explanation.walkthrough: Stockport is a town near Manchester, historically in the English county of Cheshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Stockport is a large town in north-west England, traditionally counted as part of Cheshire.

clue.text: Laze about without this?

indicators.note: 'about' suggests turning things round, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether you can lounge around idly without this.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: one lazes around for lack of the very quality the rearranged word makes.
explanation.definitionFit: Zeal is energetic enthusiasm, exactly what a person lounging idly lacks.

clue.text: Cut short excuse held up by military clique, almost over the moon!

indicators.note: cutting something short removes its end
in a down entry, raised up means read from bottom to top
held by something means held within it
almost all of a word means its final letter is dropped

blocks.note: an alibi is an excuse proving one was elsewhere
a junta is a military group ruling after a coup

explanation.surface: A flimsy excuse is accepted by the generals, who are delighted.
explanation.definitionFit: Over the moon is an idiom for delighted, and jubilant means triumphantly joyful.

clue.text: Seeing to a few mates on a binge?

definitions.text: Seeing to a few mates on a binge?

blocks.note: surface: looking after some friends
setter's reading: 'seeing to' and 'mates' in their sexual senses, during a wild bout of indulgence

explanation.surface: Someone looks after a few friends during a drinking spree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seeing to' sounds caring, and mates sound like friends; read saucily, several partners at once on a binge is a wild party.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild party of unrestrained sexual activity among several people, or any bout of excess.

clue.text: Very happy to drag round suspect being set up

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it
in a down entry, set up means raised, so read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: to lug is to drag something heavy
to suspect is to feel or sense something

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted to haul a suspect off after a frame-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suspect' looks like a noun, a person under suspicion, but it is the verb, to have a hunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Gleeful means full of delight or merriment, a close synonym for very happy.

clue.text: Hear about a new type of pen without getting excited

indicators.note: the court word sits about, that is surrounding, the remaining pieces

blocks.note: a court hears or tries a case
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
a quill is a feather pen

explanation.surface: Someone listens to a description of a novel pen, staying calm about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hear' suggests sound, but here it is a judge hearing a case in court.
explanation.definitionFit: Tranquilly means calmly and peacefully, describing behaviour that stays composed rather than agitated.

clue.text: Ladies, at first wobbly, dare to wear this for aerobics?

definitions.text: Ladies, at first wobbly, dare to wear this for aerobics?

indicators.note: 'at first' points to the opening letter of the word before it
something wobbly is unsteady, so the following letters are shaken into a new order

blocks.note: the opening letter of Ladies
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Nervous women at an exercise class pluck up courage to put on figure-hugging gear.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: the item the shaky beginners dare to put on is what aerobics classes wear.
explanation.definitionFit: A leotard is the tight one-piece garment worn for dance, gymnastics and exercise classes.

clue.text: A cheer for Henry, being extrovert

definitions.note: the word is the first half of a phrase, not a full synonym

blocks.note: first meaning: a shout of joy
second meaning: the word put before Henry to describe a loud upper-class young man

explanation.surface: A crowd gives a rousing shout for an outgoing man called Henry.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'Hooray Henry' is British slang for a loud, brash, upper-class young man.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both an exclamation of joy and the label attached to Henry in the slang for a braying toff.

clue.text: Refuse to be upset by a wigging?

definitions.text: Refuse to be upset by a wigging?

blocks.note: surface: staying calm and not getting rattled
setter's reading: a wigging is a telling-off, but also suggests a wig, hair you could literally keep on

explanation.surface: Someone stays unruffled despite being given a severe scolding.
explanation.walkthrough: A wigging is British slang for a scolding; the phrase meaning stay calm literally describes keeping your wig on.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to remain calm and not lose one's temper, and fits literally when someone is wearing a wig.

clue.text: Another half for bloke on the way home?

definitions.text: Another half for bloke on the way home?

blocks.note: surface: a man ordering a further half-pint in the pub before leaving
setter's reading: 'other half' is a spouse, waiting for the man at home

explanation.surface: A man has one more half-pint of beer on his journey home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another half' sounds like a drink order, but one's 'other half' is a spouse; a half is a half-pint in a British pub.
explanation.definitionFit: The other half is a familiar idiom for a spouse or partner, and the woman married to a man fits.

clue.text: Just started to use car in a strike, perhaps

blocks.note: runners who have just started are off
using a car means driving it

explanation.surface: A motorist has just started driving during an industrial dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strike' reads as a walkout but is a hit of the ball; in cricket the off drive sends it straight to the off side of the field.
explanation.definitionFit: An off drive is a batting stroke in cricket, an example of a strike at the ball.

clue.text: I'm back to cover some legislation somewhere in Africa

indicators.note: going back means the letters run from right to left
to cover something is to enclose it on both sides

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe
some legislation is a single law

explanation.surface: A returning official arrives to provide coverage for a piece of law in an African country.
explanation.definitionFit: Malawi is a landlocked country in south-east Africa, an example of a place on that continent.

clue.text: Tip given police HQ where charges were involved?

blocks.note: to tilt is to tip to one side
the Yard is Scotland Yard, London's Metropolitan Police headquarters

explanation.surface: A tip-off goes to police headquarters, where criminal charges are brought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charges' sounds legal, but these are knights charging at one another with lances in a joust.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiltyard was an enclosed arena for jousting, where mounted knights made headlong attacks at each other.

clue.text: For example, Dorothy's rejected heavy meal

indicators.note: what is rejected is sent back, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: e.g. is the abbreviation for 'for example'
Dot is a short form of Dorothy, with the possessive S

explanation.surface: A woman named Dorothy, for instance, turns down a filling dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Stodge is heavy, filling and often starchy food, such as a solid suet pudding.
